results.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
results.proof_sketch: The edges from {p,q} to B form K_{2,|B|}. For |B|≥3, this restricted plane embedding is bipartite and 2-connected. Euler's formula gives |B| faces, while every facial boundary has length at least four and the sum of facial lengths is 4|B|. Hence every face is exactly a 4-cycle p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p. The drawing of a component of G−({p,q}∪B), together with the interiors of its attachment edges, lies in one open face of the skeleton, so its attachments in B are among that face's two consecutive B-vertices. For |B|≤2 the assertion is immediate.

results.claim: All simple two-exit instances with at most one common exit-neighbor are linearly solvable, without assuming planarity. Put U=(N(p)∪N(q))−{p,q} and B=N(p)∩N(q). A start in {p,q}∪U wins. Otherwise, if B is empty the fugitive loses; if B={b}, let K be the component of b in G[U], and the fugitive wins exactly when N(s)∩K is nonempty.
results.proof_sketch:
A start in an exit or U has an immediate exit move. Suppose B={b}, s∉U, and s has a neighbor v_1 in K. Choose a simple path v_1,…,v_r=b in G[U]. Every v_i before b has exactly one exit edge. On reaching v_i that edge is untouched: all earlier Nemesis responses were forced at earlier path vertices. Nemesis must delete the current exit edge, since any other deletion lets the fugitive take that exit next; hence every later path edge and both edges at b survive. Upon arrival at b, one deletion cannot destroy both exit moves.

For the converse, B=∅ is handled by deleting the current vertex's sole exit edge after every move, and otherwise deleting the just-traversed edge. Let B={b}, s∉U, and N(s)∩K=∅. While b is unprepared, Nemesis deletes the unique exit edge whenever the fugitive first reaches a vertex of U−K. Any route into K must first reach a vertex outside U (there is no U-edge from U−K to K, and the first move cannot enter K); on that response, or on a revisit whose exit edge is already gone, Nemesis deletes one of bp,bq. Once b is prepared, every regular vertex has at most one surviving exit edge. Nemesis thereafter deletes that edge whenever it is incident with the current vertex, and otherwise deletes the just-traversed edge. Thus the fugitive never begins a turn with an exit edge and cannot escape. Marking U, searching G[U] from b, and testing N(s) takes linear time.

results.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
results.proof_sketch:
The three conditions give explicit wins. In (ii), move directly to an untouched b∈B; after Nemesis deletes one of bp,bq, use the other. In (iii), move to w. The three-edge sets {wb_i,b_ip,b_iq} for two gates b_1,b_2 are edge-disjoint, so one deletion spoils at most one; move to the other gate and escape.

Conversely, assume none holds. Call b prepared if one of bp,bq is deleted and dead if both are deleted. After the fugitive's first move to w, let C be its component outside {p,q}∪B. If C has no boundary gate, it contains no path to either exit and the fugitive is already trapped. Otherwise C has at most two boundary gates, and w is adjacent to at most one. Nemesis prepares that gate, or an arbitrary boundary gate if w sees none. Before another gate can be entered, Nemesis gets another deletion with which to prepare it. Whenever a prepared gate is entered, she deletes its other exit edge, making it dead. From a dead gate, the fugitive cannot move directly to another gate because B is independent. If he enters another outside component, that component contains the dead gate among its at most two boundary gates, leaving at most one new gate to prepare. Induction prevents entry into an unprepared gate. Mandatory deletion makes play finite. The conditions are testable by adjacency scans.

results.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
results.proof_sketch: Handle a start at an exit immediately and discard a possible exit-exit edge. Replace every regular-to-exit incidence vx by an edge from v to a fresh degree-one exit x_v, and remove the original exits. For every corresponding deleted-edge set and regular position, there is a path to an original exit exactly when there is a path to a fresh exit leaf: truncate an original path at its first exit, or reverse the replacement. Thus pre-escape moves, deletions, trapping, and winning strategies correspond edge-for-edge. In case (a), every relevant transformed component is a tree. In case (b), the transformed graph has maximum degree at most three because regular degrees are unchanged and every new exit has degree one. The source paper's linear-time theorem for trees and maximum-degree-three simple graphs therefore applies, and the transformation has linear size.

results.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
results.proof_sketch:
The graph is planar: draw the four internally disjoint a-b paths ab, a-p-b, a-q-b, and a-z-b as nested arcs; draw b-c-z in a face incident with bz and attach the leaf s at c.

The fugitive moves s→c. If Nemesis deletes bc, move c→z. Her next deletion can spoil at most one of the two edge-disjoint escape configurations z-a-{p,q} and z-b-{p,q}; move through the other common neighbor and then take the surviving exit edge. If the first deletion is not bc, move c→b. At the next fugitive turn, use bp or bq if either remains. If both have been deleted, those are exactly Nemesis's first two deletions, so ab,ap,aq remain; move b→a and then use whichever of ap,aq survives.

Nevertheless the tree condition fails after splitting exit incidences into degree-one exit copies. The only possible roots within distance one of s are s and c. Vertex s has only one edge. A full binary tree rooted at c cannot use regular leaf s, so its children must be b,z. Since z has no exit neighbor, its two children would have to be a,b, repeating b from the other root branch. Hence no such tree exists.

results.claim: The maximum-degree-three boundary for necessity of the binary-escape-tree condition is sharp even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. An eight-vertex witness has exits p,q, start s, other regular vertices c,a,b,x,z, and edges pa,pb,pz,qa,qb,sc,ca,cx,az,bx,bz,xz. It has maximum degree four; the fugitive wins, but after standard exit splitting neither s nor its only neighbor c roots a binary escape tree.
results.proof_sketch:
The degree sequence in the order p,q,s,c,a,b,x,z is (3,2,1,3,4,4,3,4). The cyclic orders p:(a,b,z), q:(a,b), s:(c), c:(s,a,x), a:(p,z,c,q), b:(p,q,x,z), x:(c,z,b), z:(p,b,x,a) yield the six facial walks p-a-z-p, p-b-q-a-p, p-z-b-p, s-c-a-q-b-x-c-s, z-a-c-x-z, and b-z-x-b. Thus 8−12+6=2 gives a sphere embedding.

Move s→c, and call the first deletion d1. If d1≠ca, move c→a. Escape if ap or aq survives the next deletion. If both are gone, they are exactly the first two deletions; move a→z. If zp survives the next deletion, take it; otherwise that deletion was zp, so move z→b and then use the surviving one of bp,bq. If d1=ca, move c→x. After the next deletion, use x→b if xb,bp,bq are all intact. Otherwise that deletion hit one of those three, so xz,zp,za,ap,aq are intact; move x→z, take zp if it survives the response, and otherwise move through a and use its surviving exit edge.

After exit splitting, no non-start regular vertex is pruned. Only s,c are within distance one of s. Vertex s has degree one. If a full binary tree were rooted at c, its children would be a,x. With parent c, x is forced to have children b,z. To avoid meeting z in the x-branch, a must use its two exit leaves. But z, with parent x, can choose children only among its p-exit leaf,a,b; a lies in the other root branch and b is already x's other child. Only one child remains, a contradiction. The sealed source proves necessity at maximum degree three, so degree four is sharp.

results.claim: With r regular vertices, the unrestricted two-exit game is outcome-equivalent to an r-move horizon recurrence. For regular v set W_0(D,v)=false; for t≥1, W_t(D,v) holds exactly when some surviving move vw either reaches an exit or has the property that, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit in G−(D∪{e}) and W_{t−1}(D∪{e},w) holds. A regular start s wins exactly when W_r(∅,s) holds.
results.proof_sketch: The recurrence is exactly the move-then-delete rule, so induction on t proves its bounded-horizon meaning. It remains to justify the horizon. For a winning state (H,v), let ℓ(H,v) be the least number of moves in which the fugitive can force an exit. Restoring edges cannot increase ℓ: induct on the horizon, follow the strategy in the smaller graph, and if Nemesis deletes a restored edge, regard that response in a virtual copy as deletion of any surviving smaller-graph edge; the actual successor contains the virtual successor. Choose a strategy attaining ℓ. After every nonterminal response the successor rank is strictly smaller. If a play revisited v, its later graph H′ would be a subgraph of its earlier graph H. Restoration monotonicity would give ℓ(H,v)≤ℓ(H′,v), whereas strict descent along the intervening rounds gives ℓ(H′,v)<ℓ(H,v), a contradiction. Thus no regular vertex repeats, so an exit is reached in at most r moves. Hence an unrestricted win is an r-horizon win; the reverse implication is immediate.

results.claim: The horizon recurrence gives an exact O*((27/4)^r)-time algorithm for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits, where r is the number of regular vertices, and depth-first evaluation establishes PSPACE membership.
results.proof_sketch: Starting from D=∅, every recursive nonterminal round adds one distinct edge to D and reduces t by one, so t=r−|D| and memoization visits at most r times the sum of binomial(m,i) for 0≤i≤r states; each has polynomial transition work. Delete the strategically irrelevant edge pq if present. With r+2 total vertices, planarity and simplicity give m≤3(r+2)−6=3r. Since 1≤2^r 2^(−i) for i≤r, the binomial theorem gives sum_{i=0}^r binomial(m,i)≤2^r(3/2)^m≤(27/4)^r. This proves the time bound. Depth-first evaluation needs a stack of depth at most r containing only edge masks, vertices, counters, and polynomial-size search frames, so it uses polynomial space.

final_writeup:
This is a partial resolution. I did not obtain either a polynomial-time algorithm for all planar simple two-exit instances or a matching hardness result.

A direct constructive classification settles every simple instance having at most one common neighbor of the exits, even without planarity. With no common neighbor, only a start at an exit or beside an exit wins. With a unique common gate b, mark all regular vertices U adjacent to at least one exit and find the component K of b in G[U]. A start outside U wins exactly when it has a neighbor in K. The winning construction walks through K toward b: every intermediate one-exit vertex presents an immediate threat, forcing Nemesis to spend that round deleting its exit edge, so both edges at b remain intact. If no such entry exists, Nemesis gets a free response before K can be reached, prepares b, and thereafter deletes the sole surviving exit edge at each visited boundary vertex. This gives a linear-time test.

For larger common neighborhoods, the common neighbors form a planar K_{2,k} skeleton. Its faces arrange those gates cyclically, and every remaining connected piece can touch at most two consecutive gates. This completely classifies in linear time the case in which both exits have the same independent neighborhood: the only winning configurations are an immediate gate, a gate one move away, or a first move exposing two gates simultaneously. Nemesis otherwise prepares and kills boundary gates while following the fugitive from face to face.

Exit splitting also yields two broader linear-time cases: arbitrary-degree instances whose regular core is a forest, and instances in which only the exits may have degree above three.

The seven-vertex construction shows why these results do not immediately extend to all planar two-exit graphs. A gate-gate edge combined with a small planar backup cycle lets the fugitive win although the binary-escape-tree condition fails. The eight-vertex construction sharpens this obstruction: it has maximum degree four, while the source theorem proves necessity of the tree condition through maximum degree three. Thus a general algorithm must account for state-dependent tempo, not only static escape trees.

The structural reformulation in this revision truncates the exact alternating recurrence at r moves, where r is the number of regular vertices. A rank-and-restoration argument shows that any win has a vertex-simple strategy, so the truncation is equivalent to the unrestricted game. In a planar simple instance there are at most 3r edges, and only deletion sets of size at most r need be memoized. A weighted binomial bound therefore improves the exact baseline from O*(8^n) to O*((27/4)^r), with polynomial space available by depth-first evaluation.

The unresolved core still begins with at least two common gates and permits one-sided exit neighbors, gate-gate edges or short gate connections, and arbitrary planar two-boundary pieces. The improved bound remains exponential and supplies neither the requested polynomial classification nor a matching hardness result.
